answer: {"legalDomain":"Criminal Law / Child Protection","mainAnswer":"Under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, mandatory reporting obligations apply to specific entities and authorities. Personnel of media, hotels, lodges, hospitals, clubs, studios, or photographic facilities who come across any sexually exploitative material involving a child must provide this information to the Special Juvenile Police Unit (SJPU) or the local police. Once an incident is reported, the police or SJPU must report the matter within 24 hours to the Child Welfare Committee (CWC) and the designated Special Court or Court of Session. In addition, all public and private hospitals are legally required to provide immediate free medical aid to child victims and immediately inform the police. The law provides immunity from civil or criminal liability to any person providing reporting information in good faith.","legalBasis":"According to Section 20 of the POCSO Act, 2012, personnel of the media, hotel, lodge, hospital, club, studio, or photographic facilities, regardless of the number of employees, who come across any material or object sexually exploitative of a child through any medium must inform the Special Juvenile Police Unit (SJPU) or the local police [Source 2]. Under the procedural reporting obligations specified in Section 19, as referenced in the available provisions, the SJPU or local police must report the matter within twenty-four hours to the Child Welfare Committee and the Special Court (or the Court of Session if no Special Court exists), detailing the child's care and protection needs and steps taken [Source 2]. Sub-section (7) protects informants by stating that no person incurs any civil or criminal liability for providing information in good faith [Source 2]. Additionally, under Section 397 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, all public and private hospitals must provide immediate free first-aid or medical treatment to victims of POCSO offences (specifically under sections 4, 6, 8, or 10) and must immediately inform the police [Source 4]. This content is educational in nature and does not constitute formal legal advice.","recommendedNextSteps":["Immediately report any knowledge or material involving child sexual abuse to the nearest police station or the Special Juvenile Police Unit (SJPU).","Contact the Child Welfare Committee (CWC) or child helpline services to ensure emergency care and protection for the child.","Consult a qualified legal professional or child protection authority for guidance on statutory reporting procedures and legal protections."]}

  "legalBasis": "According to the Right to Information Act, 2005, Section 5(2) specifies that when an application for information or an appeal is submitted to an Assistant Public Information Officer (Central or State), a period of five days shall be added in computing the period for response specified under sub-section (1) of Section 7 [Source 5]. For intelligence and security organisations specified by the State Government that are generally exempt, a proviso states that in the case of information sought concerning allegations of human rights violations, such information shall only be provided after obtaining the approval of the State Information Commission and must be provided within forty-five days from the date of the receipt of the request [Source 1].   "mainAnswer": "Under Indian corporate law, Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) obligations apply to companies meeting specific financial thresholds during any financial year. Eligible companies must constitute a Corporate Social Responsibility Committee of the Board consisting of at least three directors, including at least one independent director. The committee is tasked with formulating and recommending a CSR policy covering activities specified in Schedule VII, recommending expenditure, and monitoring the policy. Additionally, the composition of the CSR committee must be disclosed in the Board's report, and the amount of expenditure incurred on CSR activities must be disclosed in the financial statements.",
  "legalBasis": "Pursuant to Section 135(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, every company having a net worth of rupees five hundred crore or more, turnover of rupees one thousand crore or more, or a net profit of rupees five crore or more during any financial year must constitute a Corporate Social Responsibility Committee of the Board. This committee must consist of three or more directors, with at least one director being an independent director [Source 1]. Under Section 135(2), the composition of the CSR Committee must be disclosed in the Board's report prepared under sub-section (3) of section 134 [Source 1]. Section 135(3) mandates that the CSR Committee shall formulate and recommend to the Board a CSR Policy indicating activities to be undertaken as specified in Schedule VII, recommend the amount of expenditure to be incurred on such activities, and monitor the CSR Policy from time to time [Source 1]. Furthermore, statutory disclosure requirements specify that companies covered under Section 135 must disclose the amount of expenditure incurred on corporate social responsibility activities in their financial statements [Source 4]. {"legalDomain": "Corporate Law", "mainAnswer": "Under Indian law, the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) must initially be completed within 180 days from the date the application is admitted. If the process cannot be finished within this period, a one-time extension of up to 90 days may be granted by the Adjudicating Authority upon a resolution passed by the Committee of Creditors with at least 66 percent of the voting shares. However, the entire CIRP must mandatorily be completed within a maximum period of 330 days from the insolvency commencement date, which includes any extensions and the time consumed in legal proceedings.", "legalBasis": "According to Section 12(1) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, the corporate insolvency resolution process must be completed within 180 days from the date of admission of the application to initiate the process [Source 1, Source 3]. 

Under Section 12(2), the resolution professional may file an application to the Adjudicating Authority to extend this period beyond 180 days if instructed by a resolution passed at a meeting of the Committee of Creditors by a vote of sixty-six percent of the voting shares [Source 1]. Pursuant to Section 12(3), if the Adjudicating Authority is satisfied that the resolution process cannot be completed within 180 days, it may extend the duration by a further period not exceeding 90 days, provided that such an extension is not granted more than once [Source 1, Source 2]. 

Furthermore, the second proviso to Section 12(3) mandates that the CIRP must be completed within an overall period of 330 days from the insolvency commencement date, including any extensions granted and the time taken in legal proceedings relating to the resolution process [Source 2]. For fast track corporate insolvency resolution processes, Section 56 prescribes a baseline time limit of 90 days, with a possible one-time extension not exceeding 45 days [Source 4].

This information is provided for educational purposes and does not constitute formal legal advice.", "recommendedNextSteps": ["Determine the exact date of admission of the insolvency application by the Adjudicating Authority to compute the statutory deadlines accurately.", "Monitor whether a resolution has been passed by the Committee of Creditors with a 66 percent majority to request an extension from the Adjudicating Authority before the initial 180-day window expires.", "Track the overall duration of the process, including any ongoing litigation, to ensure compliance with the outer 330-day statutory limit.", "Consult a qualified legal professional or an insolvency professional for guidance on specific CIRP timelines and proceedings before the National Company Law Tribunal."]}
